analysis.one_liner: Charges mining companies fees and royalties and requires cleanup plans for extracting gold, silver, and other metals from public land.
analysis.headline: Despite 20 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and a subcommittee until the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1872 mining law, companies can stake claims on federal land and extract gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals without paying the government anything for the metal they take, and without fully paying to clean up the damage. This bill would have charged claim holders an annual $100 fee and new $25 location fees, imposed an 8% royalty on mineral production, required permits with reclamation plans and cleanup bonds, and closed environmentally sensitive lands to new claims. The money collected would fund cleanup of abandoned mines. The bill died in committee without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently absorb the cost of cleaning up tens of thousands of abandoned hardrock mines; communities near mines, who would get stronger water-quality and reclamation protections; and future public-land users, since sensitive lands would be closed to new claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Claims holders would pay a $100 annual maintenance fee and a $25 location fee, with all proceeds deposited in a new Abandoned Locatable Minerals Mine Reclamation Fund [S2][S3].
Production of locatable minerals would be subject to an 8% royalty on the net smelter return, ending royalty-free extraction from public land [S3].

Any mining beyond casual use would require an operations permit with a reclamation plan, hydrologic analysis, monitoring, and financial assurance sufficient to cover reclamation and long-term water treatment if the company walked away [S2][S3].

New mining claims would be barred in wilderness study areas, roadless areas, Areas of Critical Environmental Concern, sacred sites, and Wild and Scenic River lands, and no new patents would be issued except on applications filed before September 30, 1994 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies would pay fees, royalties, and reclamation bonds and would bear significant permitting and compliance costs; some of those costs would likely be passed on in metal prices, and small claimants holding more than ten claims would pay even while merely holding claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies and some small claimholders

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy: an operations permit applicant must supply hydrologic analyses, monitoring plans, accident contingency plans, evidence of financial assurance, and proof the claim is economically viable after compliance costs [S3].

The bill could discourage domestic mineral exploration and production by raising the cost of mining on federal land, an objection the hardrock mining industry has raised to every royalty proposal (widely reported; general knowledge about the policy mechanism).

Only claimants holding ten or fewer claims with under $800,000 in annual revenue may keep doing assessment work in lieu of fees; larger claimholders pay the $100 fee even on claims they are not yet mining [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are concrete: royalties and fees for land that today yields nothing, a dedicated fund for abandoned mine cleanup, and reclamation bonds so taxpayers are not left holding toxic sites. The main costs are real but borne mostly by a concentrated industry, with some pass-through to metal prices and a heavier permitting process that could slow projects. On balance the bill is a straightforward shift of hardrock mining toward paying its own way, though the small-claim exemption is narrow enough that some modest operators would face new costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee on May 16, 2002, sent to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on June 6, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Nick Rahall introduced the Mineral Exploration and Development Act of 2002 on May 16, 2002 [S1][S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources and, on June 6, 2002, to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, with executive comment requested from Interior [S5].
Twenty members cosponsored the bill, 19 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill died at the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies came out ahead: they continued extracting gold, silver, and other minerals from federal land under the 1872 law without paying royalties or full cleanup costs, and taxpayers kept bearing abandoned-mine reclamation liabilities.

for.name: Nick Rahall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 19 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including George Miller, Ed Markey, Jay Inslee, Mark Udall, and Tom Udall.

against.name: James V. Hansen
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on May 16, 2002 and never reported it or scheduled a markup; the bill was referred to a subcommittee on June 6 and died there.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Industry opposed to royalties and fees on public-land mining
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed hardrock mining reform proposals that would add royalties and reclamation requirements to mining under the 1872 law.

sides.party_line_note: All but one of the 20 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call record exists beyond the partisan sponsorship pattern.

industries.note: The bill would end royalty-free extraction of gold, silver, and other hardrock minerals from federal land by imposing a $100 annual claim fee, an 8% production royalty, operation permits, and full-cost reclamation bonds [S2][S3]. Today these companies pay nothing for the minerals they take, so the bill's direct effect is to end a subsidy they currently receive.

Claimants holding ten or fewer claims with under $800,000 in annual revenue could keep performing assessment work instead of paying the new maintenance fee [S3], but all claimholders would face the new permitting and reclamation requirements.
Reclamation plans, monitoring, and a dedicated abandoned mine reclamation fund would create demand for environmental assessment and cleanup work and finance reclamation of orphaned mine sites [S3].
